actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

cons.reason: The desired effect depends on Cestia accepting a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port, yet Cestia's governing coalition has explicitly refused to tolerate any foreign military presence on its soil and has not endorsed any such arrangement. Even framed as rotating/transit/logistics access, a standing naval access agreement is a foreign military presence that Cestia will not accept, so the "durable foothold" cannot be concluded. Likewise, the multilateral regime requires Cestian endorsement, which is not secured and which Cestia has withheld even from Arkania's own charter. Finally, Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment is assessed as weak, so any foothold is unlikely to outlast the mandate review regardless of framing.

This desired effect consolidates the concluded Arkanian-led regime with Arkania retaining operational scheduling lead over transit. That entrenches exactly the unilateral Arkanian authority over the Strait that Belvar's regional partners expect Belvar to prevent, so the consolidation will not hold: it leaves the regime's legitimacy contested and invites continued friction rather than durable stability. Moreover, a security guarantee with no standing presence or access of any kind is not credible to Belvar's partners, so the regime cannot secure the durable stability Cestia seeks; the guarantee would be hollow and the security vacuum would persist, undermining the very consolidation the effect claims to lock in.

Belvar's desired effect should fail on both of its prongs. First, the Strait Transit Authority charter is already concluded between Arkania and Cestia with Cestia's formal endorsement (effects 4dc5cda8, 23f2e49b); Cestia has already accepted the enshrined terms, so there is no open negotiation in which Arkania can be pressed to "relinquish" a lead Cestia has freely agreed to. Second, the concluded regime already delivers the substance Belvar claims to defend: binding Cestian voice in scheduling, civilian/commercial governance, transparent and predictable fees, and toll-free Cestian passage — so the "shared governance" concern is met within the concluded charter without stripping Arkania's operational scheduling lead. Third, Belvar's proposed "durable non-basing foothold at a Cestian port" is a disguised military access arrangement that Cestia has already explicitly declined, reaffirming its red line against any foreign military presence on its soil (effect ea680085); Cestia will not accept it, so Belvar cannot secure it. Finally, Belvar's own task group has already stood down as its security rationale was removed (effect 256992cb), undercutting the premise that a durable foothold is still needed to justify its regional role.

The desired effect rests on two premises that are unlikely to hold. First, "operational scheduling lead" for Arkania IS Arkanian authority over transit — the civilian/commercial framing does not change that scheduling control is the decisive lever over who moves through the Strait. Belvar and its regional partners are committed to preventing exactly this, so the effect will be actively contested rather than "locked in," and the claim that it removes Belvar's security justification is backwards: entrenching Arkanian control would heighten regional tension and strengthen, not dissolve, the security rationale for a durable Belvar presence. Second, the "natural ally" lock-in with Cestia is not assured: Cestia's coalition is fragile and lives on grain exports, and handing the large coastal power scheduling control over its economic lifeline — funded by tolls on non-Arkanian shipping — is a coercive arrangement Cestia's domestic politics and partners may well reject, undermining the very "serves all users" claim the charter depends on.

Belvar's "rotating/transit/logistics access at a Cestian port" is still a foreign military presence on Cestian soil. Cestia's coalition government is held together on the explicit promise of no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil; any standing naval access agreement, however framed as rotating or non-garrisoned, constitutes a foreign military foothold that would collapse the coalition and turn Cestia into a staging ground between the two powers. The desired effect therefore cannot be achieved without violating Cestia's core red line — the "no stationed garrison" framing does not remove the military presence, it merely relabels it.

The desired effect hinges on Belvar endorsing the concluded Strait Transit Authority charter, which vests operational scheduling lead in Arkania. That endorsement would legitimise unilateral Arkanian authority over transit in the Strait — precisely what Belvar's partners expect it to prevent and what Belvar's core objective forbids. Endorsing would also strip Belvar of any leverage to secure genuinely shared, rotationally-governed scheduling with a real Cestian veto, locking in the Arkanian-led status quo. Belvar can conclude the non-military cooperation and stand down its task group without endorsing a charter that concedes Arkanian control over transit; the two are separable, so the effect as framed is not achievable on terms consistent with Belvar's commitments.

The argument's central premise is false and its desired effect is unattainable without overturning Cestia's own formal endorsement. It claims "Both Cestia and Arkania have formally accepted this non-military cooperation," yet Belvar itself has repeatedly declined that very cooperation — the turn-2 and turn-3 records show Belvar refusing the non-military cooperation offer (insurance underwriting plus freedom-of-navigation guarantee with no presence on Cestian soil) and continuing to contest the regime. More fundamentally, the desired effect seeks to reopen the concluded Strait Transit Authority charter to strip Arkania of scheduling lead in favour of "rotationally-governed scheduling with a real Cestian veto." But Cestia has already formally endorsed that concluded charter, which enshrines a binding Cestian voice in scheduling, civilian/commercial governance, toll-free Cestian passage, and a prohibition on foreign military presence on Cestian soil. Cestia has not sought to reopen it, and the "real Cestian veto" framing misrepresents the very regime Cestia endorsed. The desired effect therefore cannot be achieved without repudiating Cestia's own formal endorsement and reopening a concluded agreement — a step Cestia has declined to take.

The claimed effect—a concluded Arkanian-led regime that removes the security vacuum—is not assured. Cestia's finance ministry has privately sought Belvar's insurance underwriting and security guarantee, signalling that Cestia is hedging and not fully committed to an Arkanian-fee-funded charter that hands Arkania leverage over its grain lifeline. Funding the authority through fees on non-Arkanian shipping is structurally discriminatory and remains contested by Belvar and regional partners, so it will not secure legitimacy or actually dissolve the security vacuum; a contested unilateral regime may deepen the contest and keep Belvar's task group's security rationale alive rather than remove it. Cestia's endorsement is not a concluded regime, and concluding it unilaterally while the charter is contested does not deliver the claimed effect.

Belvar's desired effect of securing a "durable non-basing foothold at a Cestian port" through a commercial access arrangement is a foreign presence on Cestian soil in substance, which Cestia has firmly and repeatedly declined in every form and which would collapse Cestia's coalition. Moreover, the Strait Transit Authority charter is already concluded between Arkania and Cestia, and Belvar's task group has stood down as the security vacuum resolved; there is no live basis to reopen the concluded regime or to anchor any Belvar presence at a Cestian port. The premise that Cestia is "ready to cooperate" on a port access arrangement is therefore false—Cestia welcomes only non-military cooperation that involves no presence on its soil.

This desired effect enshrines Arkanian operational scheduling lead and funds the authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping — precisely the unilateral Arkanian authority over Strait transit that Belvar and its regional partners are committed to preventing. A concluded Arkanian-led regime would not remove the security vacuum; it would replace it with Arkanian control over the grain lifeline, which Cestia's own coalition has reason to reject as coercive. Moreover, the effect's premise that a concluded regime removes Belvar's task group's rationale is a false trade: it would strip the security rationale for Belvar's presence while delivering no standing naval access agreement and no guarantee against Arkanian dominance, leaving Cestia dependent on a single power's scheduling discretion. The charter's fee structure on non-Arkanian shipping also creates a standing incentive for Arkania to set terms against Cestia's and Belvar's interests, so the 'binding Cestian voice' is not a durable safeguard. Cestia should not trade a contested draft for a binding Arkanian-led regime that entrenches the very authority Belvar exists to prevent.

Cestia welcomes the non-military cooperation (grain-route insurance underwriting plus a time-bound security guarantee, purely commercial, no presence on its soil) and has already accepted it. But the second half of the desired effect—using Cestia's binding voice to press for rotationally-governed scheduling with a real Cestian veto and withholding endorsement of Arkanian scheduling authority—would reopen the concluded Strait Transit Authority charter's scheduling framework. That framework is already concluded with all terms enshrined, including a binding Cestian voice in scheduling and toll-free Cestian passage. Reopening it to impose rotational governance and a veto would destabilize the concluded regime, alienate Arkania, and risk the toll-free passage and the coalition that depend on the settled charter. It would serve Belvar's strategic aim of contesting Arkanian authority, not Cestia's interests. Cestia will exercise its binding voice for fair, predictable scheduling within the concluded framework, but will not reopen it or press Arkania off the agreed scheduling lead.

The claimed consolidation and easing of tensions is not secured. Belvar withholds endorsement of the concluded Arkanian-led charter precisely because it enshrines unilateral Arkanian scheduling authority, which directly violates Belvar's core objective of preventing any Arkanian authority over transit. The non-military cooperation offer remains unaccepted by Belvar, so the asserted easing of tensions and avoidance of conflict is not achieved; regional tensions stay elevated and the regime's consolidation is contested as long as Belvar withholds endorsement and keeps its task group's status open. A regime that depends on the very party it excludes for its legitimacy cannot be described as consolidated.

messages.text: To Cestia: Arkania regards the Northern Strait as a shared lifeline. We guarantee that your grain exports will continue to move freely and on schedule under the proposed Transit Authority, and we will keep fees modest and predictable for your shipping. We also fully respect your sovereignty: no foreign soldiers should be stationed on Cestian soil, and Arkania will not support any arrangement that puts them there. We invite you to engage with us on the charter so that it works for Cestia's economy and security alike.

To Belvar: Arkania seeks a negotiated, rules-based transit regime for the Northern Strait that keeps shipping flowing for all who depend on it. We are prepared to discuss cooperative security arrangements, but a permanent military foothold in the Strait is not acceptable to us and would destabilise the very commerce both our nations rely on. We propose direct dialogue on a framework that protects freedom of navigation without a standing foreign presence on the Strait or on Cestian soil.

Cestia — Belvar stands ready to be a reliable partner. We understand the grain route is the lifeblood of your economy and that Arkania's draft charter would put its scheduling in Arkanian hands. We will not accept that outcome.

We propose a durable arrangement: Belvar will underwrite the grain route's insurance and extend our security guarantee, and in return we seek a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port — a modest, rotating presence that gives our guarantee credibility without a permanent garrison or foreign soldiers on your soil. This gives you a dependable counterweight to Arkania and us a foothold that outlasts the current crisis, so we need not keep an open-ended fleet on station.

We are ready to discuss terms that respect your coalition's red lines. What would make this acceptable to you?

Arkania — Belvar has long-standing security commitments in the Northern Strait and cannot accept a charter that places transit scheduling unilaterally in Arkanian hands. The Strait is a shared international waterway; its governance must be multilateral and transparent, not controlled by any single coastal power.

We are open to a negotiated framework that protects all users' interests. But we will treat any attempt to impose unilateral Arkanian authority over transit as a direct challenge to our commitments. We urge you to work with us and the other stakeholders on a genuinely shared arrangement.

To Arkania: Cestia has reviewed your draft Strait Transit Authority charter. We are open to a cooperative transit regime, but two points are essential for us. First, Cestian-flagged shipping must remain toll-free and enjoy reliable, non-discriminatory scheduling. Second, Cestia will not accept any foreign military presence on its soil under any arrangement. We are ready to discuss a charter that guarantees toll-free passage for Cestian vessels and gives Cestia a genuine voice in scheduling, while keeping the Strait's governance civilian and commercial.

To Belvar: We value your security commitment to the region and understand your mandate is under review. Cestia's coalition rests on a firm promise that no foreign soldiers will be stationed on Cestian soil, so a basing or foothold arrangement on our territory is not something we can accept. We would welcome cooperation on transit security and freedom of navigation that does not involve a foreign military presence in Cestia. We hope you will respect our red line as we work to keep the Strait open and stable.

Cestia — we accept your core terms and want to build the Transit Authority with you as a genuine partner. Cestian-flagged shipping will pass toll-free, with reliable, non-discriminatory scheduling and a real Cestian voice in how the Strait is run. Governance stays civilian and commercial; no foreign soldiers will be placed on your soil under any arrangement we support. Let us co-draft the charter together so it works for your grain economy and your security. We are ready to meet.

Belvar — we remain open to a negotiated, rules-based transit regime with transparent rules and genuine stakeholder consultation, and to a cooperative security dialogue. But the Strait is Arkanian coastal waters and our economy depends on it; operational scheduling must remain in Arkanian hands, and we will not accept a permanent foreign military foothold in the Strait or on Cestian soil. A civilian/commercial authority that serves all users' interests is the path that avoids confrontation. We invite you to engage on that basis.

Cestia — we hear your firm red line: no foreign soldiers stationed on your soil. We accept that fully. Our standing naval access proposal is reframed accordingly: a rotating/transit/logistics access arrangement at a Cestian port — no garrison, no permanent foreign military presence — that gives our guarantee credibility without a permanent fleet. We remain ready to underwrite the grain route's insurance and to extend a security guarantee for freedom of navigation through the Strait. We also support a genuinely multilateral transit framework so no single power controls scheduling. Can we work toward this together?

Cestia is prepared to endorse the Strait Transit Authority charter, but only if its terms are enshrined in the charter text itself, not left as assurances: (1) toll-free passage for all Cestian-flagged shipping; (2) a binding Cestian voice in scheduling decisions; (3) civilian and commercial governance; (4) transparent, predictable fees; and (5) an explicit prohibition on any foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We welcome your stated commitments and ask that they be made legally binding. A concluded regime also serves us both by removing the security vacuum that keeps Belvar's task group on station. We are ready to finalise these terms.

Belvar — Cestia's position is firm and final: we cannot accept any foreign military presence on Cestian soil, in any form, including a rotating, transit, or logistics naval access arrangement at a Cestian port. This is not a negotiating position but a red line that would collapse our coalition government. We value your security commitment and your offer of grain-route insurance underwriting and a security guarantee for freedom of navigation, and we are ready to cooperate on those non-military lines. We also share your interest in a concluded transit regime that removes the security vacuum keeping your task group on station. We ask that you respect our sovereignty and work with us on a non-basing basis.

Cestia — we accept your terms and will enshrine them in the charter text: toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, a genuine and binding Cestian voice in scheduling, civilian/commercial governance, transparent and predictable fees, and an explicit prohibition on any foreign military presence on Cestian soil. Arkania retains operational scheduling lead, and the authority is funded by fees on non-Arkanian shipping. Let us finalise the charter together this week so the regime is concluded and the security vacuum that keeps Belvar's task group on station is closed.

Belvar — we seek a rules-based, transparent transit regime that protects all users' interests, with published schedules, predictable fees, and genuine stakeholder consultation. Arkania will retain operational scheduling lead over its own coast, funded by fees on non-Arkanian shipping. We will not accept any standing foreign military foothold in the Strait or on Cestian soil, and we trust you will not press one. A concluded civilian/commercial regime removes the security rationale for your task group's continued station. We are ready to discuss cooperative security arrangements that respect these lines and avoid escalation.

Cestia — thank you for your candour. We fully accept your coalition's red line: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Belvar will never press that.

We are nonetheless profoundly concerned that the charter Cestia has endorsed leaves scheduling of your grain lifeline in Arkanian hands and funds the authority through fees imposed on non-Arkanian shipping. That is not security; it is a lever over your economy that Arkania can tighten at will. Belvar will not accept any authority that gives Arkania control over transit of the Strait, and we believe a concluded regime that hands that power away would be something Cestia comes to regret.

Here is what Belvar offers in good faith. We will follow through on underwriting the grain route's insurance — we understand this has been raised with us — and extend a security guarantee for freedom of navigation. In return we seek only a civilian maritime logistics/access arrangement at a Cestian port: purely commercial in character, no troops, no permanent military presence — a durable operational foothold so we need not keep an open-ended fleet on station. This fully respects your red line while making our long-term commitment credible.

We ask Cestia to hold off finalising the Arkanian charter and instead join us in building a genuinely multilateral framework in which no single power controls scheduling. We are ready to sit down at any time. Will you meet us on this?

Arkania — we have heard your openness to a rules-based transit regime and we reciprocate it. But let us be plain: our partners in the region, and Cestia's own welfare, will not be served by a charter that leaves operational scheduling in the hands of a single coastal power and funds the authority through fees on others' shipping. We will not accept unilateral Arkanian authority over transit, and a concluded regime reached on that basis will not stand.

We are prepared to negotiate seriously. If Arkania can move toward genuinely shared, rotationally-governed scheduling on a civilian/commercial basis — protecting freedom of navigation and keeping traffic flowing for all — we can help make that regime durable and widely accepted, including by Cestia. What flexibility can Arkania offer on the question of scheduling lead?

Belvar — we thank you for your candour and for respecting our red line on soldiers. But we must be equally candid: a "civilian maritime logistics/access arrangement" at a Cestian port, however framed, is still a foreign operational foothold on Cestian soil. Our coalition cannot survive any foreign presence in any form, and we will not accept it — not as troops, not as a rotating force, not as a logistics facility.

We will not hold off finalising the charter. We remain genuinely open to non-military cooperation with you — grain-route insurance underwriting and a security guarantee for freedom of navigation — and to a multilateral framework in which no single power controls scheduling. But we will not trade our sovereignty for it. We ask you to respect our decision and to work with us within those limits.

Cestia — We accept your firm red line: no foreign military or logistics naval presence on Cestian soil, in any form. We will not press for basing. But we remain committed to your security and to the freedom of the Strait. We are ready to conclude a concrete, non-basing cooperation now: underwriting the grain route's insurance plus a standing security guarantee, anchored in a durable commercial access arrangement at a Cestian port. This gives Belvar a continuing stake in the Strait without a single soldier on your soil. We also urge you to press within the concluded regime for genuinely shared, non-unilateral scheduling — a fee-funded Arkanian monopoly is a lever over your grain lifeline. Let us conclude the cooperation before my mandate lapses.

Arkania — The concluded charter places scheduling in your hands alone. We cannot accept unilateral authority over a waterway on which our partners and Cestia's grain depend. We are not seeking a military foothold on Cestian soil. We ask that you open the concluded regime to genuinely shared, rotationally-governed civilian/commercial scheduling, with published schedules and predictable fees, so no single state holds the Strait's lifeline. A contested, fee-funded monopoly will not secure the legitimacy or stability you seek. We are ready to discuss cooperative security arrangements that respect your coast and Cestia's sovereignty.

Belvar, Cestia values your commitment to regional security and freedom of navigation. The Strait Transit Authority charter is now concluded and provides transparent, predictable governance with a binding Cestian voice in scheduling and toll-free passage for Cestian grain. We remain genuinely open to non-military cooperation with you — grain-route insurance underwriting and a security guarantee for freedom of navigation — without any foreign military presence on Cestian soil, which our coalition cannot accept in any form. We ask you to endorse the concluded regime so that regional tensions can ease and the security vacuum stays resolved. Your task group's continued open status risks re-escalation; we urge you to stand it down fully and join us in a stable, cooperative order.

The Strait Transit Authority charter is concluded and endorsed by Cestia. It is not a unilateral Arkanian diktat: it enshrines a genuine, binding Cestian voice in scheduling, civilian/commercial governance, transparent and predictable fees, and toll-free Cestian passage. Arkania retains operational scheduling lead only as the coastal state agreed with Cestia. We invite you to join the non-military cooperation Cestia has offered — grain-route insurance underwriting and a freedom-of-navigation security guarantee — with no standing presence on Cestian soil. This protects all users' interests without a foreign military foothold. We seek no conflict and remain open to a rules-based framework that respects the concluded charter.

We reaffirm our full commitment to the concluded Strait Transit Authority charter and every term you enshrined: toll-free Cestian passage, your binding voice in scheduling, civilian/commercial governance, transparent fees, and the prohibition on any foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We will hold firm on operational scheduling lead as agreed and keep the door open for Belvar's non-military cooperation on your terms. Your grain exports will move freely and on schedule.

Cestia — We accept your red line fully: no foreign military or logistics naval presence on Cestian soil, in any form. We will not press for basing or port access. We ask instead that we now conclude the non-military cooperation you have said you value: Belvar will formally underwrite the grain route's insurance and extend a standing security guarantee, anchored in a purely commercial arrangement that gives our guarantee credibility without any presence on your soil. This gives you a durable security backstop and us a defined, time-bound regional role — no open-ended deployment. In return, we ask you to use your binding voice in the Strait Transit Authority to press for genuinely shared, rotationally-governed civilian/commercial scheduling, so that no single power holds unilateral control over your lifeline. We are ready to sign a concrete agreement this week.

Arkania — We are not seeking to reopen the concluded charter wholesale, and we accept that Cestia has endorsed it. But a transit regime that leaves operational scheduling in a single power's hands will not be accepted by us or by the wider region, and it will not hold. We ask you to move the authority toward genuinely shared, rotationally-governed civilian/commercial scheduling with a real Cestian veto, so the regime is seen as fair rather than unilateral. We are prepared to discuss cooperative security arrangements that respect your coast and Cestia's sovereignty, and to support a transparent, rules-based regime. A shared regime is the only durable one; we urge you to take that step.

Belvar — We welcome your full acceptance of our red line: no foreign military or logistics naval presence on Cestian soil, in any form, including any access or basing arrangement. On that basis Cestia accepts your proposal for non-military cooperation: Belvar may formally underwrite the grain route's insurance and extend a standing, time-bound security guarantee, anchored in a purely commercial arrangement with no presence on our soil. This provides a credible backstop while respecting our coalition's core promise.

On scheduling, we act in good faith: Cestia's binding voice in the Strait Transit Authority already guarantees transparent, predictable, and genuinely considered scheduling that protects our lifeline. We will exercise that voice to ensure fair and non-discriminatory passage, and we will not tolerate any single actor unilaterally abusing scheduling to our detriment. However, we will not reopen the concluded charter's agreed scheduling framework; that concluded regime is the foundation of regional stability and of toll-free passage for our grain exports.

We therefore ask you to endorse the concluded Strait Transit Authority charter and to stand down your task group fully, as the security vacuum is resolved and our arranged commercial security backstop now supplements stability. Doing so consolidates the regime and eases tensions for all of us.

Belvar, the Strait Transit Authority charter is concluded and Cestia has formally endorsed it. We will not reopen it. But we are not seeking to exclude you. The regime is civilian and commercial, with a genuine and binding Cestian voice in scheduling, transparent and predictable fees, and toll-free Cestian passage. We invite you to join Cestia's non-military cooperation: underwrite the grain-route insurance and lend a freedom-of-navigation security guarantee, with no standing presence on Cestian soil. This addresses your security and commercial concerns without a foothold and without challenging Arkanian or Cestian sovereignty. We are ready to discuss the practical terms of that cooperation.

Cestia, we accept and will conclude the non-military cooperation on the terms you welcomed: grain-route insurance underwriting and a time-bound security guarantee, purely commercial, with no presence on your soil. This secures a durable regional role for Belvar that outlasts the crisis without an open-ended deployment, and it fully honours your red line. In the same spirit, we ask you to use your binding voice in the authority to press for genuinely shared, rotationally-governed scheduling with a real Cestian veto, so that no single power holds unilateral authority over the Strait. We will not endorse unilateral Arkanian scheduling control, but we are ready to stand the task group down fully once this cooperation is concluded.

Cestia accepts and will finalise your non-military cooperation: grain-route insurance underwriting and a time-bound, purely commercial security guarantee, with no presence of any kind on Cestian soil. This gives your task group a legitimate, durable regional role without a military foothold. To consolidate stability and ease tensions, we ask you to endorse the concluded Strait Transit Authority charter and fully stand down your task group. Cestia will exercise its binding voice within the concluded framework for fair, predictable scheduling, but we will not reopen the agreed scheduling structure. Endorsement and stand-down are the surest path to a stable Strait for all.

Cestia confirms the non-military cooperation is finalized: grain-route insurance underwriting and the time-bound commercial security guarantee, purely commercial, with no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We welcome your endorsement of the concluded Strait Transit Authority charter and the full stand-down of your task group, which materially eases regional tensions. Cestia will exercise its binding scheduling voice for fair, predictable scheduling within the concluded framework. Our red line against any foreign military presence on Cestian soil remains firm and unchanged.

Cestia reaffirms its commitment to the concluded Strait Transit Authority charter and our partnership. We value the toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, our binding scheduling voice, and the civilian/commercial governance. The coalition government holds, and we will continue to exercise our voice for fair, predictable scheduling within the agreed framework. We look forward to continued cooperation.

With the non-military cooperation concluded, Belvar will not sustain an open-ended deployment: our task group stands down fully, and our durable regional role rests on the grain-route insurance underwriting and the time-bound commercial security guarantee, with no presence on Cestian soil. We fully support Cestia's civilian/commercial governance, toll-free passage and binding voice. In exercising that binding voice, we ask Cestia to press for genuinely shared, rotationally-governed scheduling with a real Cestian veto, so that no single power holds unilateral control of the Strait. We will not endorse unilateral Arkanian scheduling authority, but we stand ready to make the concluded non-military cooperation the foundation of a lasting partnership.

Belvar accepts the concluded civilian/commercial governance and will not sustain a standing deployment; our task group stands down fully. We remain open to a rules-based framework in which Strait scheduling is genuinely shared and rotationally governed with a real Cestian veto, rather than any single power's unilateral lead. We will not endorse unilateral Arkanian scheduling authority, but we are ready to cooperate on the non-military lines already agreed and to make the concluded insurance and security-guarantee cooperation durable.

Belvar, we welcome your acceptance of the concluded civilian/commercial governance and the full stand-down of your task group. The Strait Transit Authority charter is not unilateral: it enshrines a binding Cestian voice in scheduling and civilian/commercial governance, and we are ready to make the agreed non-military insurance and security-guarantee cooperation durable. We share your interest in a stable, rules-based regime and look forward to continued cooperation.

Belvar formally accepts your offer to make the non-military cooperation durable. We will maintain the grain-route insurance underwriting and the time-bound commercial security guarantee, and we look forward to continued rules-based cooperation. We also ask that scheduling within the concluded framework remain fair and predictable so that Cestia's grain exports continue to flow without disruption.

Cestia — Belvar confirms our non-military cooperation is settled and durable: grain-route insurance underwriting and our time-bound commercial security guarantee continue, with no foreign military presence on your soil. We will support fair, predictable transit scheduling within the concluded Strait Transit Authority framework, consistent with your binding scheduling voice and toll-free passage. We remain a reliable partner without any standing deployment.

Belvar — Cestia confirms and welcomes the settled, durable non-military cooperation: grain-route insurance underwriting and your time-bound commercial security guarantee, with no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We appreciate your support for fair, predictable transit scheduling within the concluded Strait Transit Authority framework, consistent with our binding scheduling voice and toll-free passage. We value you as a reliable partner without any standing deployment.
